expertInsight: Platform Developer II builds on Platform Developer I, but the questions ask you to reason through design choices. You may see code that works for one record and need to spot why it fails in bulk. Async questions can also ask you to choose between options that all appear workable, based on retry behavior or job chaining. Learn the governor limits and practice reading Apex for bulk and failure risks. Check the current exam guide for the latest credential requirements.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Platform Developer II Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: Platform Developer II is a challenging Salesforce exam. It tests how well you can read Apex and choose a sound design. Questions often ask what happens with many records, within governor limits, or when code needs to recover from a failure.
bullets: 70% to pass, or about 42 correct answers out of 60.

examFormat.heading: Platform Developer II Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Many questions ask you to review code or select an approach for a development task.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Many questions show a short code example or describe a requirement. One common pattern is code that works for one record but fails when it processes 200 records; you must identify a bulk-safe fix.
bestWayToPass: Write bulk-safe code: Do not put queries or DML inside loops. Gather records in collections and perform each operation once.
Choose the right async tool: Learn the limits and uses of Future methods, Queueable, Batch, and Scheduled Apex. Queueable supports chaining and can carry state.
Use clear code patterns: Keep one trigger per object and put its logic in a handler class. Separate data access from business logic.
Practice writing tests: Create test data, mock callouts, and use Test.startTest and Test.stopTest to run asynchronous work.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers advanced Apex development, including bulk-safe code, asynchronous processing, integrations, testing, and security. keyConcepts.h2: Platform Developer II: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Write Apex That Handles Bulk Work
blocks.body: Your Apex should work for one record and for a batch of 200. Keep SOQL queries and DML operations outside loops. Query the needed records, store them in a map or collection, process them in memory, and save changes together. A common pattern is one trigger per object with the logic in a **handler class**. This keeps the trigger easier to follow and makes the logic easier to test. On large objects, use selective queries because filters on unindexed fields can perform poorly. Remember the synchronous limits listed here: 100 SOQL queries, 150 DML statements, 50,000 queried records, and 10,000 records per DML operation.

blocks.heading: Choose the Right Asynchronous Tool
blocks.body: **Future methods** accept only primitive parameters, cannot be chained, and do not return a job ID. **Queueable Apex** accepts objects, returns a job ID, can be chained, and can keep state. Use **Batch Apex** to process large numbers of records in chunks; each chunk gets its own governor limits. **Scheduled Apex** starts work at a set time and is often used to launch a batch job. Asynchronous transactions have some higher limits, including 200 SOQL queries and more CPU time, which can make them useful when work should run outside the main transaction.

blocks.heading: Integrations, Callouts, and Events
blocks.body: A trigger cannot make a callout directly. Run the callout asynchronously, using a future method marked for callouts or a Queueable. Put endpoints and authentication in **Named Credentials** instead of storing secrets in code. The limits shown here are 100 callouts per transaction and 120 seconds total. A **Platform Event** lets one part of a system publish information for subscribers to handle separately, reducing dependence between them. **Change Data Capture** sends record change information to subscribers. In tests, use **Test.setMock** because tests cannot call an external network.

blocks.heading: Build Reliable Tests
blocks.body: Create the records your tests need instead of depending on data already in an org. **@TestSetup** can create data shared by test methods. Avoid **SeeAllData** because it makes tests depend on the org’s contents. Put the code under test between **Test.startTest** and **Test.stopTest**; this resets governor limits and runs queued asynchronous work before you check the results. Use **HttpCalloutMock** for callouts, and use **Test.isRunningTest** sparingly. Deployment requires 75% Apex test coverage, but tests should also check expected results, bulk behavior, and failure cases.

blocks.heading: Apply Security in Apex
blocks.body: Apex runs in system mode by default, so it may not follow the current user’s record access. **With sharing** respects record sharing; **without sharing** ignores it; **inherited sharing** follows the caller’s sharing context. Record sharing does not enforce field access. Use **Security.stripInaccessible** or **WITH USER_MODE** to prevent access to fields the user should not read or write. **WITH SECURITY_ENFORCED** is another option for SOQL when appropriate. Methods marked **@AuraEnabled** can be called from a front end, so validate inputs and check access inside the method.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Salesforce Platform Developer II Exam
scenarioTips.intro: For each code sample or requirement, compare the choices against bulk behavior, governor limits, and how the code handles failures.

blocks.heading: Check Bulk Behavior
blocks.body: A query or DML operation inside a loop is a warning sign. Gather records in collections and perform the operation once.

blocks.heading: Pick an Asynchronous Tool
blocks.body: Choose Queueable when you need object parameters, chaining, or a job ID. Use Batch for large volumes and Scheduled Apex for work that runs on a timetable.

blocks.heading: Choose an Integration Pattern
blocks.body: Run callouts asynchronously instead of in a trigger. Store endpoint and authentication details in Named Credentials. Use Platform Events to separate a publisher from its subscribers.

blocks.heading: Keep Trigger Logic Organized
blocks.body: Use one trigger per object and move the business logic into a handler class. Avoid designs that cause the trigger to run repeatedly.

blocks.heading: Test Behavior, Not Just Coverage
blocks.body: Create your own test data, mock callouts, use startTest and stopTest for asynchronous work, and assert the expected results.

nextCertsAfter.heading: Next Certifications After Developer
nextCertsAfter.intro: Good next steps after Platform Developer II:

sampleQuestions.question: Which design pattern creates one class instance that can be reused throughout a transaction?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Singleton Pattern creates only one instance of a class and provides a shared way to access it.
whyWrong: Factory Pattern creates objects based on input; it does not ensure there is only one instance.
Decorator Pattern adds behavior to an object; it does not limit how many instances are created.
Strategy Pattern lets code switch between algorithms; it does not control how many instances exist.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the @TestSetup annotation do?
options: Bypasses governor limits for every test method in the class
Creates test data once for all test methods in the class
sampleQuestions.explanation: @TestSetup creates data once before the test methods run. Each test method can use that data, which can make test setup more efficient.
whyWrong: @TestSetup creates records with DML; use HttpCalloutMock to mock an HTTP callout.
@TestSetup does not change governor limits. Each test method still has the standard limits.
@TestSetup does not control whether tests run in parallel. That is configured separately.

sampleQuestions.question: How can a trigger start a callout?
options: Make the callout directly in the trigger
sampleQuestions.explanation: A trigger cannot make a callout directly. Use @future(callout=true) or Queueable Apex with Database.AllowsCallouts to make the callout asynchronously.
whyWrong: Database.executeBatch starts a batch job; the batch code must still make the callout in its execute method.
A trigger cannot make a direct callout because it runs inside an active transaction.
Platform Events support publish-and-subscribe messaging; they do not remove the restriction on direct callouts from triggers.

sampleQuestions.question: What is one benefit of using Platform Events for integrations instead of traditional triggers?
options: They support loosely coupled, asynchronous communication
They handle every error automatically, with no retry logic needed
sampleQuestions.explanation: Platform Events let systems communicate asynchronously without depending directly on each other. This can make integrations easier to scale and maintain.
whyWrong: Platform Events run asynchronously; they are not meant to provide faster real-time execution.
Platform Events do not lower governor limits. Apex transactions still have standard limits.
Each subscriber still needs its own retry and error-handling logic.

sampleQuestions.question: How can a batch job start another batch job after it finishes?
options: Call Database.executeBatch from the current job’s finish method
Implement Database.AllowsCallouts and call the next job from the start method
sampleQuestions.explanation: Call Database.executeBatch from the current batch job’s finish method to start the next batch job.
whyWrong: Database.Stateful keeps instance variable values between batch execute calls; it does not chain jobs.
Database.Batchable is required for a batch class but does not chain jobs by itself.
Database.AllowsCallouts allows a batch job to make HTTP callouts; it does not chain jobs.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the Database.Stateful interface do in batch Apex?
options: Keeps instance variable values between batch runs
Allows the batch to make callouts to external services
sampleQuestions.explanation: Database.Stateful keeps instance variable values between batch executions.
whyWrong: Database.Stateful does not improve speed; it preserves state.
It does not bypass governor limits. Each batch chunk still has standard limits.
Database.AllowsCallouts is the interface used to allow callouts from batch Apex.

sampleQuestions.question: Which design pattern separates trigger code from business logic?
options: Decorator Pattern applied to each trigger by itself
Trigger Handler pattern with service classes
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Trigger Handler pattern keeps the trigger code separate from business logic, which makes the code easier to maintain.
whyWrong: Factory handles object creation; it does not separate trigger code from business logic by itself.
Decorator adds behavior to objects; it does not organize trigger logic by itself.
Singleton controls instance creation; it does not separate trigger code from business logic.

sampleQuestions.question: What can Queueable Apex do that @future cannot?
options: Chain jobs, accept complex parameters, and return job IDs
Run synchronously in the same transaction as the calling code
sampleQuestions.explanation: Queueable Apex supports job chaining, complex parameters, and job ID tracking.
whyWrong: Queueable Apex and @future have similar governor limits in most cases.
Queueable Apex is not inherently faster than @future; both run asynchronously.
Queueable Apex runs asynchronously, just like @future.

sampleQuestions.question: What security checks should Apex exposed to an LWC apply?
options: Sharing checks, with no field-level security
Field-level security, with no sharing checks, and no @AuraEnabled annotation
Use @AuraEnabled and enforce field-level security and sharing
sampleQuestions.explanation: Apex methods exposed to an LWC must enforce field-level security and sharing.
whyWrong: User-facing Apex code still needs security checks.
Sharing checks alone do not protect fields a user cannot access.
Field-level security alone does not limit which records a user can access.

sampleQuestions.question: What does the Strategy pattern let you do?
options: Swap between algorithms in separate classes
Create objects without naming their concrete classes
sampleQuestions.explanation: The Strategy pattern lets code switch between algorithms at runtime.
whyWrong: A shared single instance describes the Singleton pattern.
Event handling is often associated with the Observer pattern, not Strategy.
Object creation is handled by patterns such as Factory, not Strategy.

sampleQuestions.question: Which heap-size limits apply to Apex?
options: 6 MB for synchronous Apex, with no separate asynchronous limit
About 6 MB for synchronous and 12 MB for asynchronous Apex
sampleQuestions.explanation: Apex has a heap limit of about 6 MB for synchronous code and 12 MB for asynchronous code.
whyWrong: 1 MB is below the synchronous heap limit.
6 MB is the synchronous limit; asynchronous Apex has a higher limit.
Salesforce enforces heap limits to protect the shared platform.

sampleQuestions.question: What does Test.isRunningTest() do?
options: Checks whether code is running in a test so it can use conditional logic
Bypasses governor limits for the code that runs inside the test method
sampleQuestions.explanation: Test.isRunningTest() checks whether code is running in a test. Code can use this check for mock responses or other test-specific behavior.
whyWrong: It does not skip tests; it only detects the test context.
It does not improve execution speed.
Governor limits still apply in tests.

sampleQuestions.question: How can Apex be made available to Flow or Process Builder?
sampleQuestions.explanation: An InvocableMethod makes an Apex method available to Flow and Process Builder.
whyWrong: @AuraEnabled exposes Apex methods to Lightning components, not Flow or Process Builder.
@RestResource exposes Apex as a REST service, not as a Flow action.
A trigger runs after record changes; Flow or Process Builder cannot invoke it directly.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a common use for Platform Events?
options: Decoupled integrations, logging, and messaging between orgs
Batch processing of large record sets
Synchronous triggers that must finish in the same transaction
sampleQuestions.explanation: Platform Events support loosely coupled, event-driven systems.
whyWrong: Batch processing uses Batchable Apex, not Platform Events.
Scheduled jobs use the Schedulable interface, not Platform Events.
Platform Events are asynchronous, not synchronous-only.

sampleQuestions.question: How can you avoid creating the same test data in every Apex test method?
options: Create data separately in every test method
Use @TestSetup to create shared test data
sampleQuestions.explanation: @TestSetup creates data once for the test class so each test method can use it.
whyWrong: Creating the same data in each method repeats work and can slow tests.
Fewer assertions do not make a test run faster, and they can reduce test quality.
SeeAllData=true ties tests to org data and can make them fragile and unpredictable.
